sources.news_title: One Homecoming Weekend, Two Shootings Near HBCUs Leave More Than a Dozen Hurt
sources.text:
In the wake of this past weekend’s shooting near Florida A&M University, alumni, students, and faculty were quick to remind people the violence wasn’t on the campuses. For others, the shooting was also a call to action.
Police said Saturday’s shooting stemmed from an altercation following FAMU’s homecoming game against the University of Arkansas at Pine Bluff. The alleged shooter, a 15-year-old male, opened fire on Perry Street nearby Bragg Memorial Stadium.
Twelve people were injured in the incident, with one the victims being hurt while fleeing the scene, according to police. Six children were injured, with the youngest reportedly 11 years old, according to the city’s police department.
Former FAMU coach Willie Simmons and his wife shared their personal trauma and a call for action after the shooting. In 2021, their son Louis Tre Zanders was injured in a shooting at FAMU where he was a student.
“It’s the reason I started the gun violence initiative in 2019 and you try to make a difference and drive a message home there’s a better way,” Simmons told the Tallahassee Democrat. “But clearly not enough is being done because it’s continuing to happen across America.”
The university’s president, Marva Johnson, emphasized that the incident didn’t occur on the campus grounds, resulting in the city’s police department leading the investigation instead of FAMU Police Department.
“To our Rattler family and our surrounding Tallahassee community, I share your outrage and profound sadness at the senseless and despicable shooting that took place near our FAMU campus last night,” Johnson said in a video message to the university’s surrounding community.
The HBCU Culture Shop, a prominent Black college apparel vendor, said on Instagram that attendees ran through its Perry Street pop-up to flee the gunfire.
Also on Saturday, two men were hospitalized for non-life-threatening gunshot wounds after an altercation near Henderson Hall on Virginia Union University’s campus in Richmond, Virginia, according to police.
Avantae Brooks, 22, of Richmond, was one of the two men hospitalized and accused of the shooting. On Sunday, he was charged with attempted murder and use of a firearm in the commission of a felony in the shooting. Investigators said they believe he shot himself accidentally during the incident. The other man took himself to the hospital.
At this time, it is not known if Brooks is affiliated with the university.

A 15-year-old has been charged with 11 counts of attempted murder following a shooting incident near Florida A&M University during the homecoming weekend, which resulted in 12 injuries, including six children, the youngest being just 11.
Anthony Rivers III was taken into custody on Sunday in relation to the shooting that occurred Saturday night in Tallahassee. He faces serious charges including attempted second-degree murder and firearm possession by a minor.
In a court appearance on Monday morning, a judge ordered Rivers to remain detained. Authorities mentioned that further arrests could occur as their investigation into this frightening episode continues.
The shooting erupted around 8 p.m. near Perry and Manatee streets, just outside Bragg Memorial Stadium, after the homecoming game as crowds were gathering.
Preliminary findings suggest that a fight among acquaintances preceded the gunfire, causing bystanders to flee in panic. Notably, none of the victims were thought to have been the intended targets.
Out of the 12 wounded, six individuals were hospitalized, including one in critical condition, while five others have since been released.
University representatives emphasized that the shooting transpired near the campus rather than on its grounds, asserting that the campus itself remains secure.
Marva Johnson, Florida A&M President, expressed her outrage and sorrow over the detestable act, offering prayers for swift recovery to those affected.
Quinn Gray, the university’s head football coach, also condemned the shooting, highlighting the need to end such senseless violence, especially at events aimed at uniting the community.
Gray noted, “Homecoming represents family and celebration; no one should leave such an event under distress, particularly not children caught in crossfire.”
The police have yet to find a link connecting the shooting to the football game itself, and the investigation is ongoing as authorities pursue leads on additional suspects involved.

Eleven people were shot, and one person suffered an ankle injury while fleeing the gunfire.

The gunfire erupted shortly before 8 p.m. Saturday, Oct. 24, near Perry and Manatee streets, close to Bragg Memorial Stadium. Florida A&M, one of the nation’s largest historically Black universities, had hosted a homecoming football game earlier that day.
According to the Tallahassee Police Department, 11 people suffered gunshot wounds. A 12th person — the grandmother of one of the victims — was injured while trying to leave the area. The youngest person shot was 11 years old, and police said one victim was believed to be a Florida A&M student.
Six adults and six minors were injured. By Sunday morning, six people remained hospitalized, including one person in critical condition, while five shooting victims had been released, The Associated Press reported.
No deaths had been reported, and authorities had not announced an arrest as of the latest public update.
Police Chief Lawrence Revell said preliminary evidence indicates that an altercation involving a small number of people occurred before the shooting. Investigators believe the violence was isolated, but they were still working to determine what happened, why it happened and who was responsible.
The area was crowded with people leaving homecoming activities when shots were fired. Officers and first responders carried injured people through the crowd so they could reach ambulances and medical care.
Authorities are seeking witnesses as well as photos and video that could help investigators reconstruct the incident. Anyone with information may contact Tallahassee police at 850-891-4200 or provide an anonymous tip through Crime Stoppers at 850-574-TIPS.
Florida A&M said the shooting occurred near, rather than on, its campus and that the campus remained safe. The university’s official alert page listed Florida A&M as open and operating normally Monday morning.
The shooting struck during one of the most important annual gatherings for Florida A&M students, alumni and families. Homecoming at an HBCU is traditionally a celebration of community, culture and institutional pride, making the violence especially painful for those who traveled to Tallahassee for the weekend.

Tallahassee Democrats Promised Zero Tolerance Before FAMU Homecoming Shooting
sources.text:
Twelve people were shot or hurt blocks from Florida A&M's football stadium Saturday night, and six of the victims were children.
Tallahassee's Democratic city leadership had spent the lead up to Homecoming Week promising extra patrols and a zero tolerance approach to exactly this kind of violence.
None of it stopped a fight between two or three people from turning into a crowd of bleeding kids.
Tallahassee Shooting Erupts During FAMU Homecoming Week Near Bragg Memorial Stadium
Police say the gunfire started around 8 p.m. at the corner of Perry and Manatee streets, a short walk from Bragg Memorial Stadium.
Tallahassee Police Chief Lawrence Revell said 12 people were hurt, 11 of them from gunshot wounds.
One victim remained in critical condition, two more were seriously injured, and eight were listed as stable.
The youngest victim was 11 years old.
Revell said his officers moved in while the scene was still active and carried victims to safety themselves.
"It is especially heartbreaking to know that children are among those injured," Revell said.
Investigators believe a fight between two or three people triggered the gunfire, and as of the department's last update, nobody had been arrested.
Florida A&M said the campus itself was not the scene of the shooting and asked the public to steer clear of the area so detectives could work.
Tallahassee Mayor John Dailey called it "a truly horrific and heartbreaking tragedy" and said the community stands with the FAMU family.
Dailey, like most of Tallahassee's city government, is widely identified as a Democrat, though the city's elections are officially nonpartisan.
This Is Not the First HBCU Homecoming Shooting at FAMU
This is the second time in four years that gunfire has torn through a FAMU gathering tied to a major event on campus.
In November 2022, a gunman opened fire into a crowded outdoor basketball court on FAMU's campus, killing one man and wounding four other people.
FAMU is far from alone.
Lincoln University's homecoming was hit by a mass shooting that left one dead and six injured.
Tennessee State University saw a fatal shooting near its campus tied to homecoming crowds.
Mississippi's HBCU homecoming season has been marred by shootings at multiple schools in back to back years, prompting Mississippi Valley State and Delta State to announce extra security specifically because of what happened at other campuses.
Atlanta's HBCUs beefed up security years ago after a string of homecoming shootings made national headlines.
Tallahassee police have publicly promoted a zero tolerance safety push ahead of FAMU homecoming for years running, with road closures, extra patrols, and public safety summits bringing together police, faith leaders, and community groups.
The pattern now stretches far enough that it has a name among people who cover it: deadly homecoming weekend.
Why HBCU Homecoming Shootings Keep Happening Every Year
Kids are in the hospital tonight, and the honest answer is that nobody who studies this pattern should be surprised.
Large, loosely controlled street crowds gathered blocks away from a stadium's actual security perimeter create exactly the conditions where a personal dispute turns into a mass casualty event.
Metal detectors and police at the gate do nothing for people packed onto a public street corner a few blocks away, which is precisely where this shooting happened.
Year after year, the public safety message from Democrat-run cities and their universities is the same: extra patrols, zero tolerance, coordinated law enforcement.
The shootings keep happening anyway, because the guns and the grudges are already inside the crowd before the first patrol car ever shows up.
That gap between the promise and the outcome is worth asking about out loud, not burying under condolence statements.
A group of children paid for that gap this weekend.

sources.text:
A Florida A&M University homecoming celebration turned violent Saturday night when gunfire erupted near Bragg Memorial Stadium in Tallahassee, Florida, leaving 12 people injured, including six children.
Eleven people suffered gunshot wounds, while another person was injured while fleeing the scene, according to reports from the Tallahassee Democrat. The youngest victim was 11 years old. Early Sunday, three victims were reported to be in serious condition, including one who was listed in critical condition. At least one of the people injured was a FAMU student.
The shooting happened after the university’s homecoming football game on Oct. 24. Although the crowd near the stadium had begun to thin, hundreds of people remained around the perimeter, including people attending tailgates and visiting vendors.
As shots rang out, people scattered in different directions. A Tallahassee Democrat reporter who was in a parking lot near Wahnish Way after the game described seeing people run and hearing screams, though she did not hear the gunfire herself.
The panic continued as people tried to get away from the shooting. In a social media post, one parent said their 14-year-old daughter was injured while fleeing and was trampled in the rush. The girl saw people on the ground and stayed still until someone helped her. She later learned that both of her ankles were sprained.
“This could have been any of our babies,” the parent wrote.
Another parent described children crying as adults tried to get them to safety, saying they were attempting to pull other people’s children out of danger.
The shooting cast a shadow over a weekend that had brought FAMU alumni, students and supporters together to celebrate the historically Black university. For many in Tallahassee, the violence was especially painful because homecoming is a time for reconnecting with friends, family and the broader Rattler community.
Royle King, recently the executive director of the Tallahassee-Leon County Council on the Status of Men and Boys at the Leon County Sheriff’s Office, shared his grief after spending the day celebrating the university.
“My heart is heavy tonight,” King wrote. “To spend the day celebrating the university I love, surrounded by so many people I love, only to end the night hearing news like this is heartbreaking.”
King added that the shooting had affected the community personally. “This is home. These are our people,” he wrote, lamenting that what should have been a joyful weekend had become painful for so many.
Carlton Worthen, a FAMU graduate and pastor of Union AME Church, said he could imagine the panic as people rushed to escape the gunfire. He worried that the movement of a large crowd could have caused additional injuries and said he was praying the number of victims would remain low.
Chuck Hobbs, a FAMU graduate, commentator and columnist, said the shooting left him unable to sleep. He expressed concern not only for the victims’ physical injuries but also for the trauma experienced by people who heard the gunshots or saw others being shot.
Tallahassee Mayor John Dailey, who attended the homecoming parade earlier Saturday, also expressed support for the university community.
“This is a truly horrific and heartbreaking tragedy,” Dailey said. “Tonight and in the days ahead, the FAMU family is not alone. Our entire community stands with you.”
Florida gubernatorial candidates also responded to the shooting. Democrat David Jolly offered condolences and said he and his wife, Laura, were praying for the victims, their loved ones and the FAMU community. Republican candidate Byron Donalds, a FAMU alumnus, said he was devastated and praying for the 12 people injured, including six children.
State Rep. Angie Nixon, who is running for the Florida Senate, said the violence had shattered homecoming’s sense of community. She called the number of children among the injured horrifying and urged action and support for those affected.
Authorities were investigating the shooting Sunday. The reports available at the time did not announce any arrests or establish a direct connection between the shooting and the university’s football game.
The investigation comes as families and members of the FAMU community try to make sense of a night that was supposed to be about school pride and celebration but ended with children and adults injured and a community grieving.

Mass shooting outside Florida A&M University stadium wounds 11, including 6 children
Gunfire tore through a homecoming crowd outside Florida A&M University’s football stadium Saturday night, wounding 11 people, six of them children, in one of Tallahassee’s worst mass shootings.
The youngest of the victims was 11 years old and one is a FAMU student, police said. A 12th person, the grandmother of one of the victims, was injured while fleeing. By Sunday morning, five had been released from the hospital and six remained, one of them in critical condition, according to the Tallahassee Police Department. Officials have not released their names.
“It is especially heartbreaking to know that children are among those injured,” Tallahassee police chief Lawrence Revell said at a news conference shortly after midnight.
No one had been arrested as of Sunday morning, and the police had not identified any suspects or persons of interest. Investigators believe the shooting grew out of a physical fight between two or three people, Revell said, but the police have not said what set it off.
The gunfire erupted just before 8 p.m. ET near Perry and Manatee streets, behind Bragg Memorial Stadium. About two hours earlier, over 20,000 fans had filled the stadium to watch the Rattlers lose to Arkansas-Pine Bluff, 31-28, and the surrounding streets were still crowded with students, alumni and families.
Homecoming is one of the biggest weekends of the year at FAMU, a historically Black university of nearly 10,000 students, and a week of events had drawn alumni and families back to campus. The whole capital was busy that night, with Florida State University having hosted Georgia Tech earlier in the day and Halloween parties underway across town, the Tallahassee Democrat, part of the USA Today Network, reported.
Within seconds, Perry Street became a crush of people running in every direction, some knocked to the ground and trampled, others crouching wherever they could find cover. Jayden Dubois, a FAMU student, told WCTV that he heard gunshots and was trampled in the rush. When he got up, Dubois said, someone was lying on the ground next to him.
Officers ran toward the gunfire without knowing where the shooters were or how many people had been hit, Revell said. The crowd was so thick that ambulances and patrol cars could not reach the wounded.
“We had officers who were picking up victims and carrying them in their arms to transport because they couldn’t get through the mass of people,” he said.
The police declared the scene secure at about 9:45 p.m. ET. By then, FAMU had warned people to stay away from the stadium and Perry Street or to shelter in place if they were nearby. The university later said its campus was safe.
Detectives, sergeants and forensic teams were still combing the scene in the early hours Sunday as the department’s Violent Crimes Unit took over the investigation. The police have not offered a motive, but Revell said investigators were determined to find those responsible and get answers for the families.
Tallahassee Mayor John Dailey called the shooting a “truly horrific and heartbreaking tragedy” on social media.
“Tonight and in the days ahead, the FAMU family is not alone,” he wrote. “Our entire community stands with you.”
Tallahassee, a city of about 200,000, has endured several high-profile shootings in recent years. In April 2025, a gunman killed two people and wounded six others at Florida State University’s student union, about 2 miles from the Saturday shooting. In 2022, one person was killed and eight were wounded when gunfire broke out among a crowd outside a liquor store near the FSU campus after a football game.
Shootings have also shadowed homecoming celebrations at several other historically Black colleges in recent years. In 2024, gunfire broke out during homecoming weekend at Tuskegee University in Alabama, and a week later, one person was killed and four others were wounded during homecoming weekend at Albany State University in Georgia.
